passage:
Monday. Keya had spent the weekend on her first market report. Asif glanced through it at his desk, phone pressed to his ear, and slid it back. "Redo this. Tighter." Then he turned away to his call.
Tuesday. She rewrote the summary four times, not sure what 'tighter' meant. Was it the numbers? The length? Every time Asif walked past, she opened her mouth to ask and closed it again. At lunch Karthik, the other intern, said, "He's like that with everyone." She wasn't sure she believed him.
Thursday. She submitted the new version at 11 p.m., stomach tight, and lay awake wondering whether she'd already failed the internship, or whether Asif had simply had no time to explain.

qa.q: What one word did Asif use to say how Keya should redo the report?
Why did Keya keep opening her mouth to ask and then closing it?
qa.a: She was afraid asking would show she wasn't good enough 😰, and she couldn't tell if Asif was displeased or just busy.

qa.q: What small step could change things for Keya at this early stage?
qa.a: She could ask one specific question, like 'Is it the length or the numbers?', which is normal for an intern and would replace guessing with facts.

qa.q: What might Asif have been dealing with when he slid the report back?
qa.a: He was on a phone call and seemed rushed, so he may not have realised how little his one word explained or how it would land.

grounding: Over a week a woman intern told to redo a report with one word feels criticised, unsure if she failed or the senior is busy, and is afraid to ask.

passage: Aditi, you look exactly like I did at your age, staring at that email. Let your Zainab Aunty tell you something. I was twenty, an intern at a newspaper in Hyderabad. The chief sub-editor, Mr Reddy, pushed my first story back across the desk. 'Do it again.' Nothing else. I went to the washroom and cried, then rewrote it three times, guessing. Was my English bad? Did he think I was stupid? I was too scared to go and ask. Only months later did I learn he'd had four pages to close that night and barely read past my first line. So don't do what I did, beta. Go and ask your senior what was meant.

qa.q: What did Mr Reddy say when he pushed Zainab's first story back?
qa.a: He said, 'Do it again.' Nothing else.

qa.q: What was young Zainab afraid of as she rewrote the story three times?
qa.a: She feared her English was bad or that he thought she was stupid, and that fear kept her from simply asking.

qa.q: What advice does Zainab give Aditi, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To go and ask what the senior meant, because a busy senior's short words may have little to do with Aditi, and asking ends the guessing.

qa.q: What was that night like for Mr Reddy, as Zainab later learned?
qa.a: He had four pages to close and barely read past her first line, so his curt words came from pressure rather than judgement of her.

grounding: An aunt recalls being a young intern told to redo work without explanation, feeling criticised, unsure why, and too scared to ask.
